paragraphs.text: The Life and Deeds of the Venerable Aninas. Having gladly come for the enlightenment of your [?], reflecting, O lover of God, on those who shone through their ascetic struggles, I resolved to finish quickly, at the Lord’s command, what you had related to me. For as soon as I received what you had thoughtfully written, which, as though awakening me from sleep, urged me to compose and commit to writing the things concerning the man of God Aninas, I was gripped with great fear, but did not hesitate to begin the aforementioned composition. For what seemed good to your judgment can become a work that truly does good to those who seek good things. For even ordinary people need to be instructed by the accounts and deeds of those who ended their lives in goodness. For readings and frequent accounts of good people are accustomed to add still more strength and spur on those who practice these things, but also to restrain and not allow

those who do evil to be stirred by their own habits. For just as evil conversations corrupt good habits, so good conversations set right the consciences of those who listen, adorning and strengthening their souls. Thus your holiness did not wish in vain for us to commit to writing, in remembrance, the achievements of Aninas, who is among the saints; nor, in turn, could we have accomplished this without the help of God’s grace. For it is Christ who works all things in everyone; without him, nothing good is stirred in the conscience of those who do good. Your request was very pleasing to me, and also a rebuke and a reproach, which I truly brought upon myself, since I had not undertaken this myself earlier, before receiving the initiative from you through your appeal to us. And I considered this within myself: that your perfection will be counted worthy of blessedness because of your good intention. The blessing for a good deed will be given to the one through whom good things come about, even if many happen to be negligent about it. Everything will be credited to the one who was its cause at the beginning. Thus the account of blessed Aninas, being everlasting and filled with every blessing, It is as follows. From his early youth, while still in lay dress, in gentleness and silence, in humility and quietness of character, he was always seen to remain. The merriment of youth never stirred in him, nor did the turmoil of sinful passions, which are always active in the young. And he was so gentle and humble in heart that all who saw him marveled

at how, without any tradition handed down to him or instruction from others, he had instilled in his soul complete gentleness, so to speak. For it is fitting to say of him what is written about Moses: that he was gentler than all the people under heaven; and what was said by God: “On whom will I look, if not on the gentle and silent person who trembles at my words?” For this gift, being truly good, is offered to God by a free soul. Among all spiritual achievements, there is no virtue more beautiful than this. For just as God loathes arrogance above all shameful deeds, so gentleness pleases God above every good way of life, since even the unrighteous prince fell from the ranks of the heavenly powers because of arrogance. The fruit of pride is hateful to God, and through it he soon suffers a fall leading to destruction. For it is written, “Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord.” And for this reason, when carrying out his plan, our Lord displayed complete gentleness, so that through his humility he might defeat and condemn the self-exaltation which the prince of this world had seized for himself in hostility. Beautiful, then, and very good were the early signs shown by this labor-loving saint, who pleased God through gentleness as he began the path of righteousness. As for his body, he was smaller in stature than many. For I consider that I should not leave this unmentioned. The Gospel account says that Zacchaeus was small in stature, while also revealing the greatness of the will of this chief tax collector. How much more fitting, then, was it for me

to make this known in this account, since this very thing is not foreign to the narrative, and, prompted by the spiritual writings, to speak of the bodily stature of the one named in them. Someone looking more deeply might say that this should be made clear to him at once, when the greatness of God's power is about to be revealed: that it does not lie in the size of bodies. or in the stature of those deficient in body, God's grace dwells. Rather, it takes up residence in the souls of those who draw near to him in love. For it does not necessarily dwell in large bodies, as the words spoken by Samuel testify: “Do not look at his beauty or the height of his stature, for I have rejected him.” And again: And again, “The Lord takes no pleasure in a man's legs,” and, “Let not the strong man boast of his strength.” And what was said concerning David: that, being small, he was left to tend the sheep. For God also said, “I have found a man after my own heart.” So there is nothing surprising if this blessed man too was slight in stature, but great in soul through his love for God. For meekness appeared in him from a young age, as has already been said. And when he was fifteen years old, he was left an orphan by his parents. When this happened, as though something greatly beneficial had been done for him and doors had opened for him to the spiritual work he had long desired, he abandoned everything his parents had left him. He took no thought whatsoever for any of it, nor did he turn back, but hastened into the wilderness, keeping in his soul the Lord's saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and turns back will be fit for the kingdom of God.” So, with this conviction, to the Lord's commandments

the blessed man committed himself and went out from his father's house after being left an orphan, without turning back or wishing to arrange his property in any way. Instead, he went out as the straight path of the Gospel commands, according to what the apostles said: “See, we have left everything and followed you.” As he left his parents' house, he did not even wish to take bread sufficient for a single day's food, for he had heard the Lord's saying: “Do not worry about tomorrow.” Therefore he cast every care behind him, so that he would not carry a heavy burden, in accordance with the law. Wishing to travel the troubled paths of the deserts, Saint Aninas entered the inner wilderness and found a certain holy man living in a monastery, who also deserves to be remembered with honor, named Caiun, living in great abstinence and poverty, for God alone. And when he went in to him, he found nothing except what the man wore to cover his body. Having duly reflected on the saint’s life and on monastic life, he made a request to him, asking to be accepted by him. He received him and instructed him with spiritual words. And for many years the two of them practiced the same abstinence. Sometimes they wasted themselves away with great hunger, and at other times, for lack of bread, they spent many days without food, as though in the wilderness. Often, enduring hunger for a full forty days, they willingly went without food or drink. And amid such bodily affliction and extraordinary deprivation, they continued rejoicing as though at a royal banquet. They had no water at all where they lived, but carried it from the River Euphrates, which was five or

four miles away from them, once every several days, since they did not always need it. For they drank little, in keeping with their meager food. After they had spent many years living together and shining in their way of life, the blessed Aninas undertook greater abstinence, surpassing that of his teacher, devoting himself to hunger and much unceasing psalmody and to standing in prayer throughout the night—in short, pursuing complete perfection in God. Seeing all this, his teacher recognized that he was entirely spiritual, and that day by day he was rising higher through his swift progress in righteousness. He resolved to leave, leaving him alone to grow courageous and strong in the struggles of virtue. He reasoned that he ought neither to receive service from such a spiritual young man as from a disciple, nor, in turn, would the young man bear to receive service from him as from his teacher. He should therefore give him room to live by himself, so that he himself could remain unharmed, without being served by someone who had become greater in good deeds, and the young man would remain free from stumbling, and [?] those handed on to him by him, the works pleasing to God, [?]. But none of the wild animals posed any challenge to him. In those days strangers began coming to his dwelling, for his name had become renowned among the monks, all those living nearby. Almost every day, so to speak, many people came to him and benefited from what they saw of his abstinence and hunger. and remaining in great humility, and the teachings they heard from him. For this reason

he was compelled thereafter to live in his monastery and no longer roam the wilderness, but to heal those who came to him, both brothers and strangers, so that they would not seek him without finding him and become distressed and saddened at failing to meet him. He himself would also suffer loss by not healing those who had undertaken so much hardship for his sake. From then on, therefore, he took care not to leave the monastery and go elsewhere, but to wait for those who came to him and heal them with all diligence and fear of God. But since water was scarce where he lived, and in particular there was no drinking water at all, and more and more strangers came to him because of the sweet fragrance of his name, he made a very small cistern to collect rainwater for himself and the poor, or also for the brothers who were catechumens in that same monastery and lived a similar way of life. But as the strangers who stayed with him continually increased day by day, coming from every village because of his lofty and good way of life, the water lasted only a few days. For when all the water had been drawn out, some people arrived in the very heat of the day, having come for prayer, to greet the holy man, and to see him. He ordered one of the brothers to run to the little cistern and bring water for those who had arrived thirsty from their journey. But the brother said that the little cistern had no water at all. The brother was certain of this, since just a little earlier, with his own hands, he had taken the very last of the water and brought it to the strangers who had come to him. When the righteous man heard this, he raised his hands to heaven and said gently and quietly to the brother, “Go in the name of the Lord, and I trust that you will find

water.” He went, opened the door of the little cistern, and found it full. Amazed and awestruck, he glorified God, drew water, and brought it to the thirsty people, telling them of the miracles of God that had occurred. He set that miracle [?], and from then on prepared water by his own labor for strangers to drink. He made a water vessel suited to his strength. Without laziness and with a serene face, he carried water from the River Euphrates on his shoulders, and those who came to him drank it. He did this at night, beginning to carry it in the evening and continuing until dawn, without ceasing his singing, but continually carrying it on. along the whole way. He rejoiced as he sang, no less than David, believing for this reason that God was with him. Thus the stranger nourished himself with spiritual songs while carrying a water jar on his shoulder. Nor did he neglect his spiritual service, for he performed it with his tongue, so that he would neither diminish his bodily service to travelers nor abandon his spiritual work. For he took care of both, striving to refresh those who were distressed with a cup of cold water, and to please God with spiritual song. He spent seventeen years undertaking such labor, performing this work night and day with a vigilant soul and with love, serving travelers. One day, after receiving some who were unusually weary, he took up the water jar and began walking along the path to the river. Before he had reached the halfway point, the water jar was found to be full of water. Immediately he took it down and set it on the ground, knelt, wept, and prayed. Then he rose, lifted his hands to heaven, and thanked God. Taking up the water jar, he returned to his monastery. The travelers who had come to him, seeing that

he had returned without reaching the river, thought that he had fallen ill and could not reach the Euphrates as was his custom. One of the brothers ran to meet him, to take the water jar from him and go to draw water from the river in his place. When he reached the holy man, he found that the water jar on his shoulder was full of water. The brother was astonished and returned, reporting this very thing. They gathered together and were filled with amazement, and, marveling at what had happened, they glorified God. They all sprang up and met him with his hands raised to heaven, glorifying the giver of good things. But the holy man set down the water jar, weeping bitterly and begging them not to make it known, but to keep silent about what had happened. He said these words: “God’s grace did not perform this miracle for my sake, for I am a poor and sinful man, but for your sake as travelers, so that you might be comforted.” But they did not wish to remain silent, but rather to speak. And they said, “The miracles that we heard were performed by the blessed Elijah, we now see accomplished by your hand.” After that time, Patricius, the bishop of blessed memory, having learned of this, of the city of Neocaesarea. For by his visit he made the monastery renowned. And since the holy man himself carried water from the River Euphrates at night, and he honored the man for his way of life, for this very task he gave him a donkey to carry water for the strangers who came to him, so that he would not himself have to endure the toil of carrying water. Now a certain poor man came to the monastery at that time, weeping and sobbing, and said that his creditor was close at hand, but he had nothing with which to pay his debt. The righteous man took pity on him and, having nothing else, gave the donkey

to the poor man and said, “Go, sell this and free yourself from your debt.” A little later the venerable Bishop Patricius came, and after greeting the holy man, he did not find the donkey. When he learned that it had been given away, and for what reason, he brought another donkey and said to him, “Here, I give you this to keep, but when I want it and need it, let me take it back.” He did this so that he would not give this one away as he had the first—which indeed happened. For when another poor man came, weeping just like the first, being likewise in debt and having nothing with which to pay it, the faithful servant of God gave him that donkey too. Being a lover of God and devout, and loving and honoring such a way of life, that same blessed Bishop Patricius, although he was poor, took the work in hand and relied on hope in God for things beyond his means. He made a large and remarkable basin for rainwater in the monastery, capable of holding a great deal of water, which stands to this day. While it was being built, a certain chief officer named Sergius, [?] among the civic authorities then governing Neocaesarea, suddenly became deaf and mute and paralyzed throughout his body because of an unclean spirit dwelling in him. Those carrying him could not put him on a donkey, so they made a stretcher and carried him on their shoulders to the righteous man. And on that very first day, by the grace of God, strengthening his fingers with the sign of the cross, the righteous man put them into the sufferer’s ears. He immediately made the deaf man hear. Then he moved to his mouth and, in the same way,

made the sign of the cross, opened his mouth, and made him speak at that very moment. But the demon remained, tormenting the old man no less, frequently throwing him to the ground and afflicting him. And [?], breaking his bones. And the venerable bishop saw him suffering this, as did the craftsmen building the cistern, the workers, and the clergy, and all the strangers who were there at that time. And he continued suffering like this for many days. For one day, when the primicerius came to inspect the construction work, he arrived and fell there, foaming and convulsing, so that all the craftsmen and workers and the others watching fled and left the old man alone. The bishop summoned the holy man, took him by the hand, and said to him, “Set this old man free, for he has been here for many days, so mercilessly tormented and convulsed by the hostile demon, suffering throughout his body, and he has become so weak that he has no hope of life from human help.” But the servant of God, with gentleness and modesty, quietly said to the bishop, who was the chief priest, “Would any of those of lower rank dare to do or accomplish such a thing?” Then the bishop shed tears and, deeply moved, kissed the righteous man’s head and right hand. He himself pleaded with him reverently and gently, and turned and said, “Do not hide whatever the grace of God grants you, but show this mercy to this old man too.” And the holy man took the old man and went into the small [?], which was then in the monastery, built as a refuge for visiting brothers because of the Saracens. There was also a little church in it, where he sang the nighttime hymns and other hymns. There, then, once again

the demon seized the old man and threw him to the ground, and began uttering blasphemies through his nostrils and mouth and wickedly and shamefully reviling the righteous man, who was saying to him, “Come out of him.” While this was happening, Julian, of blessed memory, who had formerly been bishop of the city of Neocaesarea, arrived, along with John, son of Theodore, who was then a subdeacon, and some others. The demon would suddenly rise up, looking arrogantly at the servant of God and blowing into his face, spitting on him and beginning to seize him with his hands. But he said to him gently and quietly, “Come out of him, for you will not be allowed to remain in him, enemy of God and of the truth.” But he shook the man and stared shamelessly at the servant of God, saying, “Do you command me to come out? I cannot come out of him unless I blind his eyes.” And I will break his arm and leg and make his whole body invisible. I will not come out of him. The righteous man said to him, “Be sure that you come out and do not harm a single one of his limbs. Or will you leave him injured?” And the ancient enemy, the demon, persisted in saying these things, while the righteous man continued to give the same answer. Finally, the demon said to the servant of God, “At least give me permission to go out through these doors.” The righteous man said to him, “Go out through the doors as you wish, and be driven away into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” And immediately he went out, throwing the doors wide open, and was driven away by the power of the cross. While the healed man was still lying on the ground, the servant of God turned and beckoned to the previously mentioned subdeacon John. He called him over and said

to him, “Look, the man appointed chief officer in this elder’s place is coming to visit him, with some soldiers accompanying him. But do not let them see the elder lying like this, without dignity and covered in dirt on the ground. For there was not even a plank beneath him, nor a reed mat, nor anything else usually found in a hut, but only bare earth. Go out and keep them waiting a little while, until the elder receives complete healing. Then they may come in to him.” The attendant went out and saw no one in the first courtyard. But when he reached the second, he found Philotheus—for that was the name of the man who had become chief officer in the elder’s place— and the others, who had dismounted from their horses. He kept them waiting a little while so that they would not go in. Then the subdeacon went in with his arms stretched out and raised toward heaven, marveling and glorifying God, who reveals to those who do his will deep mysteries and such glorious things, and who had revealed to the righteous man, who saw not with bodily eyes but with divine eyes, the impending arrival of those coming to visit the elder. Then the servant of God gave the man his hand and raised him from the ground. He dusted off his head and clothes, which were all covered with dust, and seated him there in that little church. He gave orders that those who wished to come in to him, see him, and speak with him should be allowed to enter. And the healed man, whose name was Sergius, remained there for many days after his healing, giving thanks and praise and proclaiming Christ our God, and marveling at the righteous man’s boldness before God. He was sent away in peace.

And he returned to his own place, coming often to the saint and giving thanks and praising the Lord’s name. God had granted him the power to heal various kinds of sores and wounds. From everywhere, the sick and those suffering from injuries gathered around him. So did those tormented by an evil demon. God’s grace healed them all through his hands. The saint decided that it was necessary to step on all those who came to him because of their afflictions. For he believed that all afflictions and all bodily wounds came from Satan, who is truly the relentless enemy of the human race. And he trusted in the Lord’s word, which promised [?] to give his followers authority to walk on snakes and scorpions and over all the enemy’s power. For this reason he trampled on loathsome and venomous afflictions, placing his hope in Christ our God. When those suffering from various afflictions learned of his custom, they entrusted themselves to him so that he would do this to them. Rejoicing and full of faith, they threw themselves down before him so that he might step on them, hoping that healing would be given to their bodies through the soles of his feet. And this often happened through God’s power. For many wealthy men suffering from disease in their feet, unable to endure the suffering and pain of medical treatment, begged him to step on them and received an immediate cure. This caused many to marvel and say in awe, “This disease has never been cured except in the days of the holy apostles.” Women also came

to him with hidden ailments that physicians could not see. Sick and worn down by their long suffering, they fell at the saint’s feet, seeking to be deemed worthy of being stepped on according to his custom. Immediately their hidden afflictions disappeared, and they rose, strengthened with genuine and lasting health. Their faces were radiant, though before they had been haggard and darkened by their afflictions. They praised God, who is above all, for giving such a gift to the saint. He made no distinction between the rich and the poor. Nor did he ever listen to the powerful with greater respect than to the poor and weak. Instead, he received everyone who came to him equally, with love in God, bearing the burdens of them all. For he cared for each person as for himself, and was pulled in every direction by many people, so that he would turn his attention to them. Although he suffered distress from this, he never said anything in vexation or showed distress on his face at the commotion around him. In the region of Apamea there was a monastery. In it there was a certain man who led an angelic life. A way of life like that of the wise Simeon he had adopted, for he stood on a pillar. In those same parts some robbers were hiding. Since there was an abundance of wealth in the monastery, they dug under the wall at night and entered the monastery. After breaking everything apart, searching everywhere, and finding nothing, they turned their furious rage against one another. But one of them, wishing to quench his accomplices’ frenzy, picked up a stone from the ground

and hurled it at the holy man’s head, wounding him so severely as to accomplish the deed he intended. The righteous man wanted to come down from the pillar. But Saint Aninas immediately learned of this very thing from the Holy Spirit and called a lion that regularly served him. He set plenty of food before it and said to it, “Eat your fill, for you are about to set out on a long journey.” Then he asked for a sheet of parchment and wrote on it as follows: “Father, it was revealed to me that, after suffering an attack by robbers, you wish to come down from the pillar, feeling obliged to take a momentary revenge. But restrain that impulse, so that you do not lose the reward for your labors, that is, the eternal kingdom.” Then he tied it around the beast’s neck and sent it away, commanding it, “Do no harm to anyone passing along the road.” The beast rushed toward the monastery to carry out what it had been commanded. Those who happened to be on the road, seeing it from afar coming at a headlong run, thinking that they lay exposed to the beast’s attack, to be devoured. But he, as though driven by a shepherd, went along at the saint’s command, harming no one. When he came to the monastery and scratched at the doors with his claws, one of those living there came out and saw him. He ran and told his teacher, saying, “An enormous beast is standing before the doors.” After saying a prayer, he replied, “Brother, open the door for him, so that he may come in.” Once the beast was inside, he braced his front feet against a pillar and raised his neck toward the holy man, offering the letter to the holy man. He took it and read it,

and marveled at the revelation about this that had come to the saint, and at the obedience of wild beasts. And after glorifying God, he abandoned the undertaking he had planned as an act of revenge. Along with such great miracles, which we have recounted with reverence for God, I thought it especially fitting not to overlook this most glorious miracle either, particularly since it is well able to sanctify your hearing. A certain woman, who had adorned herself with piety and was living as a stranger in some remote parts of the desert, fell victim to a terrible disease. Having lost hope in ordinary physicians, she prayed to God that, once healed, she might be granted the opportunity to reach the saint, so that, seeing him, she might take delight in the saint’s angelic life. And soon, after only a short time, she obtained what she had prayed for and set out on the journey before her. Now pagan Saracen robbers were accustomed to roaming in that great desert. One of them, carrying a spear, happened to meet the woman. He had an untamable will. Immediately he thrust his spear into the ground, seized her, and searched her. Finding that she carried nothing except a little food, enough for her journey, he turned his thoughts to a shameful act. Seeing herself subjected to prolonged torment and wishing to escape this assault, she raised her eyes to God and called upon the saint for help, so that he might deliver her from the man. Immediately trembling and blindness seized him, so that he no longer dared to torment her further. Instead, leaving her lying on the ground, he tried to pull out the spear with his hand and turn back.

to flee to his own people. But it, having taken root in the ground, would not let him flee at all. As he struggled for a long time to pull out the spear, he was struck by an evil spirit and began, in full view, binding his hands behind his back, to turn back to expose his wicked undertaking, barking like a dog, and foaming at the mouth, with his hair standing out in the air. He ran up to the saint, confessing his audacious deeds. The saint extended his usual compassion to him as well, and, after praying to God, granted him immediate healing. Having come to his senses after being freed from the demon, and seeing the extraordinary [?] of the deed—how the weapon that had been meant to help him had taken root in the ground and remained there to expose him—he sought refuge in saving baptism, the sinful blindness that had previously settled in him being what he understood he could wash away through it. The woman, having enjoyed the blessing of prayer, returned home, glorifying God for all the miracles performed by the great passion-bearer through his devotion to God. The man who had previously been a fierce pagan, but was afterward tamed by the gift of holy baptism, then stayed with him, having come to love the monastic life. And the spear driven into the ground took root, remaining an immovable testimony against his sin, preserved in that place to this day, the greatness of the miracles that the saint continually performed being proclaimed by it forever. After some time had passed, and as deeds were being accomplished through the gift of the Holy Spirit by God's servant Aninas, the former governor Trocondus,

having been stricken with paralysis, set out from the great city of Antioch, to come to that vast desert and receive healing from the man of God. But when he reached the city of Chalcedon, his condition became very serious, and he could no longer continue onward, as his affliction grew more severe and grievous. He sent men who were rulers and dignitaries to the saint, begging him to take the trouble to come to the city of Chalcedon. They came and spoke to the saint, but, not obtaining what they sought, they hurried to the venerable man of blessed memory, Bishop Patricius, believing that he could persuade the righteous man. and put the request into effect. And immediately the blessed bishop Patricius himself came to the monastery. With men of high rank he pleaded with the servant of God. But the latter was greatly distressed, since, having once withdrawn, and shut himself away in the wilderness, he had never gone out from it anywhere. When evening came, he answered them, saying, “If the Lord wills, I will answer you tomorrow.” Very late in the evening a messenger arrived, sent by that Trocondas, who said to Patricius, “Do not trouble the holy man or compel him to leave his monastery. For he himself will come.” And immediately, after one day, he came with a multitude of commanders, treasurers, and governors, and dignitaries, and with countless soldiers following them. He arrived with his whole body contracted and his face twisted. But through the grace of the crucified Christ, the righteous man had only to touch him, and a considerable part of his face straightened. For the holy man anointed him with the oil of grace and gave

him his own staff, commanding him to walk not only within the monastery but also a considerable distance around it. The man who had previously been unable to move came to love walking, so that he went far enough away to see Neocaesarea and the river Euphrates. During that interval a certain Palatius arrived, who was from the imperial city and was traveling from Apamea. After his departure from the great city of Antioch, he had been struck by an evil spirit and remained mute and motionless. He reached the monastery of the man of God with his wife, sons, and daughters, and the rest of his household servants. Those carrying him brought him into the monastery and laid him at the holy man’s feet. After praying over him and taking some oil from the lamp, he put his fingers into the mouth of the man lying there, and anointed his tongue and the other parts of his mouth. He said to him, “Say, ‘Glory to you, O God.’” He did say it, but neither distinctly nor clearly. The holy man did the same again, saying to him a second time, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” And he spoke these words a little more clearly. And again, a second and a third time, he made him pronounce more fully and clearly the words, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” While these things were happening, all the dignitaries and governors who were with the nobleman Trocondas were there. And they saw everything that was happening. Then, while the sick man lay there, motionless and paralyzed, he took oil from that same lamp, and, anointing him with the sign of the cross like a skilled physician, he began to rub the oil into him, starting from

his heels and proceeding part by part as far as his head. He did the same on both sides of his body, and gave him his hand before all the people. For not only was the house of prayer itself filled, large though it was, but all the surrounding buildings were filled with people watching what was happening. He raised him up, and, taking him by the hand, made him walk with him. At first he staggered and swayed from side to side, but when his limbs had grown strong and he was completely healed, he gave him his own staff, saying, “Take this and walk.” And when the righteous man let go of him, he walked on his own, glorifying God, and with him all those who had witnessed such a very great miracle. And they glorified the one who grants such things to those who fear him. But Tricon neither reflected on God's love for humanity that had been shown to him, nor called to mind the healing from illness that he had received, but, distressed and hostile, he kept considering how he too might immediately be completely healed and fully restored to strength, like Palatinus, who had been healed at the same time as he was. He said that the miracle that had happened to Palatinus was an illusion and a deception. When he uttered this blasphemy against the truth, his body immediately became paralyzed, and was given over to its former lifelessness. Later, however, he made inquiries about Palatinus, and found that he was a distinguished man, with many servants and a wife of noble birth, and that he was acknowledged by the many commanders who were with him. From this he became convinced that Palatinus would not take part in mockery or wrongdoing. Reflecting on his own unbelief, he began to weep over his former unbelief.

And he remained there a long time, begging the saint to accept him in his repentance and concern, and pleading with him to pray for him. so that he might receive mercy from God. And the saint, praying more earnestly and striving more intensely, prayed to God for him, asking him to overcome the man's wickedness through his love for humanity. And with much effort he succeeded in entreating God to heal him. There was also with Tricondus Trajan, one of the most illustrious men, who was commander of the Isaurian people. He summoned Theophilus, the devout priest, and showed him one of his followers who was severely tormented by an unclean spirit. He asked him to take the man and bring him to the saint, and to ask him to free the man from his affliction. And that devout man did so, and brought the man to the righteous one. Looking at him and examining him, he said to the priest, "This man cannot be healed, for he is sexually immoral and a drunkard, and the demon will certainly strangle him." And indeed, as the righteous man had foretold, the next morning before dawn the wicked demon attacked and strangled that man, and he was buried there. After some years, there was brought to his monastery Arnaeus, who held authority in Calliope and lived in the great city of Antioch. He suffered from a disease of his feet and was carried in a sheet, since he could neither walk nor endure medicinal herbs being applied to his feet. The saint healed him by God's grace and the power of the crucified one, and he remained in the monastery for many days, walking and glorifying God. After his healing he lived for more than nine years, which he spent in good health, without suffering any affliction from the disease of his feet that he had previously had. Glorifying God for the healing granted to him, he brought a horse,

well-fed and used to racing in chariot races. At that time this Arnaeus was governor of the great city mentioned earlier. He brought this horse to the monastery to grind grain to feed the strangers who came there. Although this horse was fierce, savage, and unruly, the holy man of God took it with his own hands and, together with its healed master, harnessed it to the millstones. And as though it had long been accustomed to this and had grown up doing it, it adapted so meekly and ground grain, that because of this everyone marveled all the more at the glorious miracles performed by God's servant. In addition to all the others, another glorious miracle was performed by Christ's faithful servant. A young bull, brought as an offering to God and fed there, became wild when a wicked demon entered it. And it was so stirred by anger that it neither recognized its herdsman nor spared anyone else, but sought to destroy everyone it came across. Having broken free from its tether and escaped from the enclosure, it roared and raged wildly, attacking those who met it. And it rushed into the inner courtyard and entered the kitchen, attacking the brothers who were working there, preparing enough food to refresh the guests. Thus, out of fear of the young bull, they were forced to throw themselves into the bread oven, choosing rather to burn in the fire than to be gored by it, for they saw its boundless frenzy. But God, who loves humankind, kept them unharmed amid the fiery flames, extinguishing the fire through the righteous man's prayer. All the others, terrified of the young bull, climbed onto the roofs of the stables.

The righteous man, hearing the noise of those fleeing, asked what had caused this commotion. He was told that the young bull, filled with rage, had broken out of the stable and was chasing everyone so fiercely that it had even entered the kitchen. When the holy man heard these words, he raised his hands to heaven, offered a prayer, and went to meet the young bull. Those standing on the roofs of the stables, seeing him hastening toward the young bull, felt pity for the righteous man and tried to stop him with their shouts, telling him to avoid the young bull's anger and frenzy. But the righteous man answered no one, and, strengthened by his faith in God, approached the young bull and touched it with his hands. Calming its anger with gentle words, he took hold of it with his hand and led it into its own stable, to the manger. Thus everyone marveled and was awestruck at the indescribable miracle performed by the holy man, and they glorified God, who reveals his power through those who fear him. I know that, even before I speak, you all know and have heard of Sergius, who was appointed chief of the tribe of the Sauraites, a man of noble birth, in Osrhoene, and who exercised authority in Mesopotamia, from the Saracen border. Through his feats of valor, and being braver than anyone else, he won victories every year over the destructive Persians and the Saracens who aided them, and he so thoroughly defeated them. so that he not only barred them from every entrance into Greek territory beyond their own borders, but also harassed them there and drove them out of their own land. They had been defeated by him in many ways and could not resist his prevailing power, knowing his invincibility

and that they could not stand against them in battle. Only one course remained to them for devising their deliverance: they recognized the magical skill of their own people. And immediately, through their sorcery, they summoned the demon they worshiped in the form of an idol and sent the spirit against the man in the form of a snake. It entered the man’s bosom and tormented him, causing him unceasing pain. Distressed by the demon that was attacking him and tormenting him, he immediately hastened to a quiet haven, God’s holy man. The saint received him with his holy hands and, taking oil from the lamp, anointed his whole body, while the sufferer showed and indicated where the spirit was crawling, nesting within him like a snake. For whenever the saint’s hand touched him, the spirit fled into another part of his body. And again, when the saint’s hands reached there, it immediately moved into another part. Finally, after the glorious Sergius had spent many days in fasting and prayer, he was able to drive the demon out of him completely. And when the man had grown very strong and become well, he restored him to his former strength. [?] against those who had risen against him through sorcery, the God-hated Saracens. Then an angel of the Lord came down from heaven and appeared to the saint in the form of lightning. He came to him and stood in the air, raised about three cubits above the ground. He remained standing in that place for many hours, saying or declaring nothing, but simply standing there, looking nowhere, neither to one side nor the other. And so he ascended into heaven. The saint quickly went to where the angel had stood and traced the sign of the cross, and built a little church there,

which remains to this day. While he was staying there one year, before the trenches were dug, great crowds gathered at the saint’s monastery, faithful people coming from everywhere. Most of them were sick and had come to see him and receive a blessing, and they obtained healing. For the surrounding regions loved him with true faith. On that day a large crowd gathered, larger than usual. It was harvest time. As there were many people, they became very thirsty and found themselves in great distress. The holy man was grieved in his soul and wept, saying, “Alas for me! What if the Lord should call me, sinful and wretched as I am, to account for the distress of these people who have come to me?” Sighing gently, he raised his hands to heaven and spoke these simple words in a loud voice: “Lord God, give them water.” As soon as he spoke, a small cloud appeared above the people and poured down heavy rain only over them and around them. There was an abundance of water among them and only in their immediate surroundings. The people drank their fill of water and glorified God, the giver of all good things, for he fulfills the wishes of all who fear him, hears their prayer, and saves them. This became known to everyone in the surrounding area. They gave all the more thanks to God that such a gift had been given to their region. Many believers came to him from everywhere, although they had no affliction or illness, wishing only to see him and receive a blessing from his holiness. Others, likewise, though not driven by any bodily affliction, threw themselves at his feet so that he would tread on them, so that [?]

pagan [?]. To learn about the glorious things that had happened concerning the two of them, eyewitnesses of these things came and praised God for everything, who, through the occasion of bodily suffering, had brought even the Greek to know his truth, so that the power of Christ God might be evident everywhere through his servants, bestowing various gifts of grace on souls and bodies. The holy man had also been given another gift: divine revelations. For his pure and sinless soul foresaw hidden things at all times through the grace of God who dwelt in him. But because of his humility of soul, which he had always willingly joined to his earthly body, he did not wish to disclose the things about his disciples that were revealed to him. The revelations became evident to everyone through circumstances such as these. When the Saracens were about to take them captive, he would gather the brothers and the strangers beforehand. Weeping and crying aloud, he would say to them, “Children, pray to God, that he may deliver these lands from the approaching troubles.” Again, when a famine was about to occur, he would prepare his disciples for prayer ahead of time. Although he himself had no desire at all to disclose anything of what was revealed to him, they themselves knew, since experience had taught them, that he was moved by a revelation to urge them to pray. Often, too, when some of the brothers were about to die, he would call each one aside before he fell ill, and say, “Child, take care of your soul, and pray often to the Lord, asking him for mercy.” When asked why he was saying this, he would reply, “It is good always

to pray and to please God.” For he did not wish to disclose a single one of the things revealed to him, guarding himself in his great humility so that there might never be in him any cause for boasting or for pride, which God hates. One day, as the holy man was standing on the stairway of the [?], after the church service, a bright cloud suddenly covered him and the whole [?]. A voice came from the cloud, like thunder, rumbling for a long time. The [?] itself shook like fruit tossed by a strong wind. The sixty brothers who were on the [?] were alarmed and fled out of the [?], crying out fearfully to the holy man about what had happened. The holy man instructed and comforted them, saying, “Do not be alarmed or afraid, children, and do not be terrified. Instead, prepare your hearts to do the Lord’s will every day.” Immediately the [?] stopped shaking, the cloud passed away, and the voice fell silent and could no longer be heard. All the brothers approached and fell at his feet, begging him to tell them the reason for that terrifying vision. He said to them, “Children, this is what is most important and worth seeking: that one should please God and cleanse one’s soul of every defilement.” and from the deception of this world, and from all plundering and desire for possessions. And let him establish his soul in the love of God, like a firm foundation, unshaken by the wind. For asking about mysteries is unnecessary and unsound, brothers. Strengthen yourselves and love one another, for God is loved in human beings. As blessed John said: “Whoever does not love his brother, whom he can see, how can he love God, whom he cannot see?”
